item.mechanism: Solid solution hardening occurs because Cr atoms with smaller atomic radii dissolve into the BCC lattice, causing severe lattice distortion and generating dislocations, which increases hardness and strength.
item.system: HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 (4.2 at% Cr added to HfMoTaTiZr)
item.operating_conditions: As-cast state, room temperature compression testing
item.supporting_observation: XRD analysis shows lattice parameter decrease from 3.392 Å to 3.325 Å, and hardness increases from 460.1 HV to 535.8 HV.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the dissolution of Cr in the BCC phase of this specific alloy system; does not claim to apply if Cr forms only precipitates without solid solution.
item.alternatives_considered: The text notes that brittle intermetallic phases usually deteriorate plasticity, but here the solid solution effect is cited for strength enhancement.
quotes: Cr also has the smallest atom radius among constitute elements of HfMoTaTiZr.
incorporating Cr into the existing BCC unit cell will lead to more severe lattice distortions and more dislocations
solid solution hardening, which effectively promotes the hardness and strength of HfMoTaTiZr.

item.mechanism: The formation of a hard intermetallic Laves phase contributes to strength enhancement through dispersion strengthening.
item.supporting_observation: The presence of the Laves phase correlates with a 56.96% increase in hardness compared to the reference alloy.
item.scope_limits: The text states that generally, brittle intermetallic phases deteriorate plasticity, implying this mechanism alone would reduce ductility.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors consider the general rule that brittle phases lead to a decline in ductility, which is counteracted by the specific morphology.
quotes: The Cr addition in this work leads to the formation of a hard intermetallic Laves phase, which has a positive impact on the hardness and strength
Generally speaking, the appearance of the brittle intermetallic phase usually deteriorates the plasticity
Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength

item.mechanism: A reticulated (continuous network) structure of the Laves phase hinders crack propagation, thereby compensating for the ductility loss typically caused by brittle phases and improving overall fracture strain.
item.supporting_observation: Fracture surfaces show ductile dimple fracture in the Laves phase and quasi-cleavage in BCC grains, with the reticulated structure impeding crack extension.
item.scope_limits: Relies on the specific volume fraction (3.8%) and continuous morphology; the text implies this does not hold if the phase is granular or discontinuous.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors contrast this with the typical behavior where brittle phases cause intergranular fracture and cleavage.
quotes: the Laves phase is connected and forms a reticulated structure.
Such a unique structure is expected to hinder crack propagation during deformation and compensate for the loss in plasticity
During deformation, the extension of cracks was impeded by the reticulated structure of the Laves phase

item.mechanism: Cr addition reduces the density of the alloy while maintaining or improving mechanical properties, addressing the high density of the base HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
item.supporting_observation: Experimental density of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 10.26 g cm⁻³ compared to 10.44 g cm⁻³ for HfMoTaTiZr.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the substitution of heavier elements with lighter Cr; not tested for other light element additions.
item.alternatives_considered: The text mentions the need to reduce density without sacrificing properties, implying other strategies might fail to do both.
quotes: Thus, a strategy should be developed to reduce the density of HfMoTaTiZr without sacrificing its good mechanical properties.
Among various elements, Cr is of particular interest as it is lighter than elements in HfMoTaTiZr.
It is expected that alloying Cr in HfMoTaTiZr can not only reduce the density but also increase the room temperature mechanical properties

item.mechanism: The Laves phase forms as a complex multicomponent intermetallic (Cr2(Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta)) due to the stability of Cr-X binary systems, rather than a simple binary phase.
item.supporting_observation: XRD peaks for the Laves phase do not match standard binary Cr2X patterns, and EDS shows Cr dominance with other elements present.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the Cr addition in this specific multi-component system; not claimed for other alloying elements.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors initially considered binary Cr2X phases but rejected them based on XRD mismatch.
quotes: Cr can form various Laves phases with the constituent elements in HfMoTaTiZr such as Ti, Zr, Hf, and Ta
we speculate that the Laves phase should be a complex multicomponent intermetallic phase

item.mechanism: Microstructural segregation leads to dendritic regions enriched in high melting point elements (Mo, Ta) and interdendritic regions enriched in lower melting point elements (Hf, Ti, Zr), influencing local properties.
item.supporting_observation: EDS analysis shows dendrite arms have higher Mo/Ta content while interdendritic regions have higher Hf/Ti/Zr content.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the as-cast microstructure resulting from vacuum arc melting; heat treatment might alter this.
item.alternatives_considered: Not stated, but the text attributes the asymmetry of XRD peaks to this compositional difference.
quotes: The dendrites are enriched in high melting point elements: Mo (2610 °C) and Ta (2996 °C)
the interdendritic regions are mainly composed of elements with relatively lower melting points: Hf (2222 °C), Ti (1668 °C), and Zr (1852 °C).
The shape of the (200), (211) and (220) peaks are asymmetric due to the compositional difference between dendrite and interdendrite regions.

item.mechanism: The fracture mode shifts from intergranular/cleavage (brittle) in the base alloy to quasi-cleavage in BCC grains and ductile dimple fracture in the Laves phase in the Cr-added alloy.
item.supporting_observation: SEM images show river patterns and intergranular fracture in HfMoTaTiZr, while HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 shows dimples in the Laves phase.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the observed fracture surfaces; does not quantify the exact stress thresholds for mode transition.
item.alternatives_considered: The text contrasts the two fracture modes to explain the difference in ductility.
quotes: HfMoTaTiZr exhibits intergranular fracture and cleavage fracture mode
HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 RHEA shows a quasi-cleavage fracture surface at BCC grains.
ductile fracture is observed for the Laves phase, since its grains display the dimple fracture

item.mechanism: The improvement in ductility of the base HfMoTaTiZr alloy in this study compared to previous literature is attributed to slight compositional differences detected by XRD.
item.system: HfMoTaTiZr (this study vs Juan et al.)
item.supporting_observation: Fracture strain in this work (11.6%) is 65.5% higher than Juan et al., correlated with lattice parameter differences.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the comparison with Juan et al.'s alloy; not a general mechanism for all HfMoTaTiZr variants.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors do not propose other mechanisms for the base alloy's ductility improvement, focusing on composition.
quotes: Considering the observation by XRD, it is speculated that the improved ductility or ε f of HfMoTaTiZr is attributed to the slight compositional difference from that of Juan et al.
The lattice parameter of HfMoTaTiZr prepared in this work is larger than that by Juan et al.
The yield strength ( σ 0.2 ) of HfMoTaTiZr in this work is 1543.1 ± 40.9 MPa, which is consistent with that in ref. [20]
